screens.title: What is Software Architecture?
screens.narratorSegment: Before we write production code, we need a plan that shapes the whole system. Software architecture is that plan: the organization of components, their relationships, and the principles guiding design and evolution. Think of architecture as the blueprint for a house or city planning for a town; it fixes major choices early and makes later development predictable and manageable. In practice, architecture decides whether you build a single monolith or a set of microservices, what quality attributes you prioritize, and which technologies or platforms align with project goals. This matters because architectural decisions are often costly to change once implemented. A poor architecture can lead to a tangled codebase, slower delivery, and unhappy users and teams. Good architecture manages complexity, aligns technical decisions with business goals, and makes trade-offs explicit. As you progress through these slides, you will learn how architecture differs from software design, how to weigh functional versus non-functional requirements, and what a software architect actually does day to day. Keep in mind: architecture is strategic, not glamorous. It is the difference between a structure that grows sustainably and one that collapses under change. What long-term outcome do you want your architecture to enable?

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These learning objectives map to the strategic skills you need when planning a system. First, you will be able to define software architecture and explain how it differs from software design in scope and impact. That means recognizing when a decision changes the system's structure versus when it governs implementation details inside a component. Second, you will explain why architecture matters across the development lifecycle: how a good architecture reduces technical debt, enables scaling, and provides a shared vocabulary for stakeholders. Third, you will identify the key characteristics and concerns architects address, like performance, scalability, reliability, maintainability, and security — and how these are often in tension. Fourth, you will understand the role and responsibilities of a software architect, from selecting major platforms to mentoring teams and documenting trade-offs. Each objective includes a small mnemonic to help you remember the skill and a verified competency milestone so you can measure progress. Keep these objectives in mind as questions you should answer by the end of the chapter: can you explain a trade-off, and can you choose a structure that supports the project goals?

screens.title: Defining Software Architecture
screens.narratorSegment: Software architecture is the fundamental organization of a system: its components, their relationships to one another and to the environment, and the principles guiding design and evolution. Put differently, architecture records the significant structural choices that have long-term impact. A useful way to understand this is with an analogy: an architect plans the layout and structure of a building, specifying load-bearing walls and utility corridors, while builders and designers choose finishes and room-level details. In software, choosing microservices versus a monolith, selecting a communication style like events or synchronous calls, or deciding to centralize data are architectural choices. Design focuses on how parts inside that structure accomplish tasks, such as implementing a particular algorithm in a module or applying a design pattern like a Factory Method. A common misconception is that architecture is only documentation; in fact, it is a set of decisions that guide implementation, testing, and operations. For example, choosing a distributed cache to meet latency goals is architectural because it affects deployment, consistency, and failure modes. Key takeaway: define architecture as strategic, durable decisions and design as tactical, local solutions. A good question to ask: which changes would force you to rewrite the system versus which would require only local edits?

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Defining Software Architecture
Definition
The fundamental organization of a system and the principles guiding its evolution.
Core definition
Architecture describes components, their relationships, interactions with the environment, and the governing principles. It makes strategic choices that are costly to change later.
Analogy
Building blueprint vs. interior finishes.
Common misconception
Architecture is not only documentation; it is a set of decisions that shape implementation and operations.
Example
Choosing microservices or a monolith is an architectural decision because it affects deployment, team boundaries, data ownership, and operational complexity.
Key Takeaway

Architecture = strategic structure; design = tactical implementation within that structure.

Check your understanding
Name one architectural choice and explain which parts of the project it will influence beyond code changes.

screens.title: Architecture vs. Design
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the difference between architecture and design helps avoid misplaced effort. Architecture is system-scoped and strategic: it sets the shape, the major components, and constraints that affect long-term cost and evolution. Design is module-scoped and tactical: it focuses on algorithms, classes, and patterns used to implement features inside that structure. Consider the example of an online learning platform. Choosing separate services for user management and course catalog is architectural because it affects deployment, cross-service communication, and data consistency. Choosing JWT for session tokens is a design decision inside the authentication service; it affects implementation and local security mechanisms but does not force a system-wide restructuring. A key misconception is to treat every technology choice as tactical — selecting a database type or cloud provider can be architectural when it constrains data models, scaling approaches, and operational practices. Use a simple mental check: will this decision require re-architecting the whole system if changed? If yes, it's architectural. If no, it's likely a design decision. Takeaway: clarity about scope prevents wasted rework and anchors trade-offs during planning. Architecture vs. Design means ask whether changing a decision would force system-wide changes. if yes, it's architectural; if no, it's design.. In practical terms, how scope, impact, and timescale differ. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Architecture vs. Design
Architecture vs Design
Compare scope, timescale, and consequences.
Architectural choice
Example: Splitting the system into microservices. Consequences include independent deploys, cross-service communication, and data partitioning decisions.
Design choice
Example: Selecting JWT for tokens inside authentication. Consequences are local to the service: token format, validation, and rotation policies.
Quick test
Ask: Will changing this decision force reworking multiple services and deployment scripts? If yes, classify it as architectural.
Misconception
Not every platform choice is tactical. Selecting a database style or cloud provider can be architectural when it shapes data models and operational practices.
Key Takeaway

Use scope as your guide: strategic = architecture; local = design.

screens.title: Components, Relationships, and Environment
screens.narratorSegment: A software architecture view always names three things: components, their relationships, and their environment. Components are the major parts of the system — services, databases, user interfaces, and external integrations. Relationships describe how those components interact: synchronous calls, message queues, shared storage, or event streams. The environment includes platforms, cloud providers, and external services the system depends on. An architect documents interfaces and contracts between components so teams can build independently and reason about failure modes. For example, in an online learning platform, components might include a user service, course catalog, and enrollment service. Relationships could be an event bus for notifications and a REST A P I for catalog queries. The environment could be a chosen cloud provider and managed database services. A common pitfall is forgetting operational concerns: network latency, failure isolation, and monitoring. Architecture ties components to operational practices — deployments, scaling patterns, and disaster recovery. Concrete exercise: identify three components in a familiar app and list the relationships and environmental constraints that influence them. This practice reveals assumptions that should be explicit in your architecture. Components, Relationships, and Environment means an architecture names components, describes relationships, and defines environmental constraints for correct operation and evolution.. In practical terms, the building blocks of an architectural view. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Components, Relationships, Environment
Architecture elements
Components, relationships, and environment form the architectural view.
Components
Identify major services, data stores, and external systems that deliver business capabilities.
Relationships
Document communication styles: synchronous APIs, asynchronous messages, shared databases, and event streams.
Environment
Capture platforms, cloud constraints, network assumptions, and operational services like monitoring or CDN.
Concrete example
For an online learning platform: components = user service, course catalog, enrollment service; relationships = API calls for queries, event bus for enrollment notifications; environment = managed database, cloud region, CDN for assets.
Common mistake
Designers sometimes omit environmental constraints like latency or availability, which leads to unrealistic assumptions during implementation.
Key Takeaway

Make components, relationships, and environment explicit to reveal assumptions and operational risks.

screens.title: Non-Functional Requirements (NFRs)
screens.narratorSegment: Non-functional requirements — also called quality attributes — describe how well a system performs its functions. Common NFRs include performance, scalability, security, reliability, maintainability, and usability. Architects prioritize and balance these attributes because they often conflict. For instance, optimizing for extreme performance may reduce maintainability or increase cost. Conversely, designing for maintainability might accept some performance overhead to keep the codebase understandable. To make these priorities actionable, architects translate NFRs into measurable constraints: response time targets, uptime percentages, throughput goals, and acceptable recovery times. A concrete example: if your platform must support 10,000 concurrent learners with a median response time under 300ms, that requirement drives choices about caching, database sharding, and autoscaling. A frequent misconception is treating NFRs as afterthoughts; when left undefined, they become implicit and lead to misunderstandings and rework. Ask stakeholders to rank quality attributes early and convert them into measurable targets. Closing question: which two quality attributes would you prioritize for a public-facing learning platform, and what measurable target would you set for each? Non-Functional Requirements (NFRs) means quality attributes must be prioritized, measured, and translated into design constraints that shape structural decisions.. In practical terms, quality attributes that shape architecture. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Non-Functional Requirements (NFRs)
Quality attributes
Performance, scalability, security, reliability, maintainability, usability.
Why they matter
NFRs drive architecture because they determine constraints on components and interactions. They often require trade-offs and measurable targets.
Performance
Latency and throughput targets.
Scalability
Handling increased load gracefully.
Security
Protecting data and access.
Concrete example
Requirement: support 10,000 concurrent users with median response time under 300ms. Architectural choices: caching, sharding, autoscaling, and CDN for static assets.
Misconception
Treating NFRs as optional or vague leads to unstated expectations and late rework.
Key Takeaway

Translate NFRs into measurable targets early and use them to guide structural decisions.

screens.title: Architectural Trade-offs
screens.narratorSegment: Architectural trade-offs are everywhere because improving one quality attribute often degrades another. The essential skill is to make trade-offs explicit and aligned with business goals. A classic example is performance versus maintainability: inlining optimizations might speed a hot path but make code harder to understand and change. Another is consistency versus availability in distributed systems — choosing strong consistency can increase latency or reduce availability during partitions. Architects should surface these tensions, present options with consequences, and obtain stakeholder alignment. Use a simple trade-off template: name the attributes in tension, describe the options, list consequences for cost and operations, and recommend an approach with a fallback plan. A misconceived approach is to optimize for every attribute simultaneously; that leads to over-engineering and wasted effort. Instead, prioritize based on measurable business outcomes — for a learning platform, prioritize availability and reasonable latency during peak hours, while accepting some complexity in data replication. Close with a question: which trade-off would you prioritize for a global learning service, and what fallback would you accept if traffic spikes unexpectedly? Architectural Trade-offs means make tensions visible, evaluate consequences, and align priorities with business goals rather than chasing perfect scores on every attribute.. In practical terms, balancing competing quality attributes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Architectural Trade-offs
Balancing quality attributes
List tensions, evaluate options, and choose with business alignment.
Trade-off template
  1. Name attributes in tension.
  2. Describe architectural options that favor each attribute.
  3. List consequences for cost, operations, and future change.
  4. Recommend a prioritized approach and a fallback plan.
Concrete contrast
Performance vs maintainability: optimize hot paths with caching and tuned queries when necessary, but document and isolate optimizations so code remains readable and testable.
Warning
Trying to maximize every quality attribute usually leads to unnecessary complexity and cost.
Key Takeaway

Prioritize attributes based on business needs, document trade-offs, and plan fallbacks.

screens.title: Role and Responsibilities of a Software Architect
screens.narratorSegment: A software architect is more than a senior coder. They act as a bridge between business goals and technical implementation. Core responsibilities include defining the overall system structure, selecting technologies and platforms, identifying major components and their interfaces, and setting architectural principles and standards. Architects also evaluate trade-offs, document rationale for decisions, and mentor development teams to maintain architectural integrity. They often coordinate cross-team concerns like security, backup strategies, and operational practices. A common misconception is that architects only create diagrams and hand them off; the reality is continuous engagement: reviewing designs, guiding implementation, and adjusting architecture in light of new information. For example, an architect might recommend a managed database service to reduce operational burden while designing a data partitioning strategy to meet scalability targets. Another responsibility is making change affordable: by defining boundaries and contracts, architects enable teams to evolve components independently. Closing thought: the most effective architects combine technical judgment with communication skills — can you describe a decision you would document and how you would explain its trade-offs to a product owner? Role and Responsibilities of a Software Architect means architects translate business goals into structural choices, set standards, and mentor teams to keep systems coherent and evolvable.. In practical terms, what architects do beyond writing code. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Monolith vs Microservices — A Practical Contrast
screens.narratorSegment: Two common architectural patterns are monolithic and microservices, each with clear pros and cons. A monolith places most functionality in a single deployable application. It simplifies local development, testing, and reduces operational surface area. However, it can become hard to scale certain parts independently and may slow team velocity as the codebase grows. Microservices split functionality into smaller, independently deployable services. This enables independent scaling and clearer team ownership but increases operational complexity: service discovery, network failure handling, and cross-service data consistency become significant concerns. A useful practical test for choosing between them is to ask whether teams need independent release schedules and whether scaling needs are uneven across modules. For a small team and early-stage product, a monolith often accelerates delivery. For a large system with distinct domains and growth in different areas, microservices can reduce long-term friction. A common misconception is that microservices are a silver bullet; they solve some problems and create others. The key is to align structural choice with business objectives and team capabilities. What criteria will you prioritize for your project and why? In practical terms, when to choose one structure over the other. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Making Architectural Decisions
screens.narratorSegment: Effective architectural decisions follow a repeatable process: gather requirements, identify constraints, evaluate options against quality attributes, select an approach, and document rationale. Start by collecting functional requirements and the non-functional targets we discussed earlier. Identify hard constraints like budget, regulatory rules, or mandated platforms. Next, generate feasible options and evaluate them by how well they satisfy prioritized quality attributes. For each option, list operational consequences and costs. Select an approach that aligns with the highest-priority business outcomes and include a rollback or mitigation strategy. Finally, document the decision: the chosen option, the reasoning, measurable targets, and where assumptions may break. This documentation helps future teams understand why a choice was made and when to revisit it. A common mistake is skipping documentation — undocumented decisions become hidden technical debt. Example: choosing a managed message queue because it reduces operational effort but noting the cost and vendor lock-in as trade-offs. Decision process
A practical six-step flow to make and record architectural choices.

screens.title: Activity: Architectural vs Design Decisions
screens.narratorSegment: This activity asks you to practice classifying decisions as architectural or design. Work through each scenario and explain your reasoning. Scenario one: choosing a microservices architecture with separate services and a message queue. This is architectural because it changes deployment, cross-service contracts, and operational needs. Scenario two: selecting JWT for session management inside the authentication service. This is a design-level decision: it affects implementation within a component rather than the overall system structure. Scenario three: storing user data in a NoSQL database while course content lives in a relational database is architectural because it imposes long-term constraints on data modeling, queries, and migration strategies. Scenario four: defining the interface for a CourseRepository class is a design decision inside a service. Scenario five: selecting a cloud provider for hosting services is architectural as it affects operations, cost, and platform capabilities. For each scenario, write one sentence explaining why changing the decision later would be costly or not. This exercise builds the habit of evaluating the impact scope of choices and capturing assumptions early. After classifying, ask yourself: what information would make me reconsider this classification?

fullNarratorScript:
Before we write production code, we need a plan that shapes the whole system. Software architecture is that plan: the organization of components, their relationships, and the principles guiding design and evolution. Think of architecture as the blueprint for a house or city planning for a town; it fixes major choices early and makes later development predictable and manageable. In practice, architecture decides whether you build a single monolith or a set of microservices, what quality attributes you prioritize, and which technologies or platforms align with project goals. This matters because architectural decisions are often costly to change once implemented. A poor architecture can lead to a tangled codebase, slower delivery, and unhappy users and teams. Good architecture manages complexity, aligns technical decisions with business goals, and makes trade-offs explicit. As you progress through these slides, you will learn how architecture differs from software design, how to weigh functional versus non-functional requirements, and what a software architect actually does day to day. Keep in mind: architecture is strategic, not glamorous. It is the difference between a structure that grows sustainably and one that collapses under change. What long-term outcome do you want your architecture to enable?

These learning objectives map to the strategic skills you need when planning a system. First, you will be able to define software architecture and explain how it differs from software design in scope and impact. That means recognizing when a decision changes the system's structure versus when it governs implementation details inside a component. Second, you will explain why architecture matters across the development lifecycle: how a good architecture reduces technical debt, enables scaling, and provides a shared vocabulary for stakeholders. Third, you will identify the key characteristics and concerns architects address, like performance, scalability, reliability, maintainability, and security — and how these are often in tension. Fourth, you will understand the role and responsibilities of a software architect, from selecting major platforms to mentoring teams and documenting trade-offs. Each objective includes a small mnemonic to help you remember the skill and a verified competency milestone so you can measure progress. Keep these objectives in mind as questions you should answer by the end of the chapter: can you explain a trade-off, and can you choose a structure that supports the project goals?

Now let’s attach concrete examples and success checks to each objective so you can verify understanding. For defining architecture, you should be able to point to an architectural decision: choosing microservices instead of a monolith, and explain why that is strategic rather than an implementation choice. For lifecycle importance, you will explain a scenario where poor architecture led to high maintenance costs, and contrast it with a case where a clear architecture enabled fast scaling. For key concerns, you should name at least three non-functional requirements and describe a trade-off involving them, for example scalability versus maintainability. For the architect role, you will outline responsibilities: selecting platforms, defining interfaces, and mentoring teams. Each milestone asks you to give one example and one short justification. These checkpoints help you move from recognition to application, and they create a clear path from learning to verified competency. Keep these milestones in mind as short tasks to practice after each lesson.

Software architecture is the fundamental organization of a system: its components, their relationships to one another and to the environment, and the principles guiding design and evolution. Put differently, architecture records the significant structural choices that have long-term impact. A useful way to understand this is with an analogy: an architect plans the layout and structure of a building, specifying load-bearing walls and utility corridors, while builders and designers choose finishes and room-level details. In software, choosing microservices versus a monolith, selecting a communication style like events or synchronous calls, or deciding to centralize data are architectural choices. Design focuses on how parts inside that structure accomplish tasks, such as implementing a particular algorithm in a module or applying a design pattern like a Factory Method. A common misconception is that architecture is only documentation; in fact, it is a set of decisions that guide implementation, testing, and operations. For example, choosing a distributed cache to meet latency goals is architectural because it affects deployment, consistency, and failure modes. Key takeaway: define architecture as strategic, durable decisions and design as tactical, local solutions. A good question to ask: which changes would force you to rewrite the system versus which would require only local edits?

Understanding the difference between architecture and design helps avoid misplaced effort. Architecture is system-scoped and strategic: it sets the shape, the major components, and constraints that affect long-term cost and evolution. Design is module-scoped and tactical: it focuses on algorithms, classes, and patterns used to implement features inside that structure. Consider the example of an online learning platform. Choosing separate services for user management and course catalog is architectural because it affects deployment, cross-service communication, and data consistency. Choosing JWT for session tokens is a design decision inside the authentication service; it affects implementation and local security mechanisms but does not force a system-wide restructuring. A key misconception is to treat every technology choice as tactical — selecting a database type or cloud provider can be architectural when it constrains data models, scaling approaches, and operational practices. Use a simple mental check: will this decision require re-architecting the whole system if changed? If yes, it's architectural. If no, it's likely a design decision. Takeaway: clarity about scope prevents wasted rework and anchors trade-offs during planning. Architecture vs. Design means ask whether changing a decision would force system-wide changes. if yes, it's architectural; if no, it's design.. In practical terms, how scope, impact, and timescale differ. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A software architecture view always names three things: components, their relationships, and their environment. Components are the major parts of the system — services, databases, user interfaces, and external integrations. Relationships describe how those components interact: synchronous calls, message queues, shared storage, or event streams. The environment includes platforms, cloud providers, and external services the system depends on. An architect documents interfaces and contracts between components so teams can build independently and reason about failure modes. For example, in an online learning platform, components might include a user service, course catalog, and enrollment service. Relationships could be an event bus for notifications and a REST A P I for catalog queries. The environment could be a chosen cloud provider and managed database services. A common pitfall is forgetting operational concerns: network latency, failure isolation, and monitoring. Architecture ties components to operational practices — deployments, scaling patterns, and disaster recovery. Concrete exercise: identify three components in a familiar app and list the relationships and environmental constraints that influence them. This practice reveals assumptions that should be explicit in your architecture. Non-functional requirements — also called quality attributes — describe how well a system performs its functions. Common NFRs include performance, scalability, security, reliability, maintainability, and usability. Architects prioritize and balance these attributes because they often conflict. For instance, optimizing for extreme performance may reduce maintainability or increase cost. Conversely, designing for maintainability might accept some performance overhead to keep the codebase understandable. To make these priorities actionable, architects translate NFRs into measurable constraints: response time targets, uptime percentages, throughput goals, and acceptable recovery times. A concrete example: if your platform must support 10,000 concurrent learners with a median response time under 300ms, that requirement drives choices about caching, database sharding, and autoscaling. A frequent misconception is treating NFRs as afterthoughts; when left undefined, they become implicit and lead to misunderstandings and rework. Ask stakeholders to rank quality attributes early and convert them into measurable targets. Closing question: which two quality attributes would you prioritize for a public-facing learning platform, and what measurable target would you set for each? This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Architectural trade-offs are everywhere because improving one quality attribute often degrades another. The essential skill is to make trade-offs explicit and aligned with business goals. A classic example is performance versus maintainability: inlining optimizations might speed a hot path but make code harder to understand and change. Another is consistency versus availability in distributed systems — choosing strong consistency can increase latency or reduce availability during partitions. Architects should surface these tensions, present options with consequences, and obtain stakeholder alignment. Use a simple trade-off template: name the attributes in tension, describe the options, list consequences for cost and operations, and recommend an approach with a fallback plan. A misconceived approach is to optimize for every attribute simultaneously; that leads to over-engineering and wasted effort. Instead, prioritize based on measurable business outcomes — for a learning platform, prioritize availability and reasonable latency during peak hours, while accepting some complexity in data replication.
